title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: At the end of the winter, in the Shtcherbatskys' house, a consultation was being held that was to pronounce on the state of Kitty's health and the measures to be taken to restore her failing strength. She had been ill, and as spring came on she grew worse. The family doctor gave her cod-liver oil, then iron, then nitrate of silver, but as the first and the second and the third all did no good, and as his advice when spring came was to go abroad, a celebrated physician was called in. The celebrated physician, a very handsome man, still youngish, asked to examine the patient. He maintained, with a peculiar satisfaction, it seemed, that maidenly modesty is a mere relic of barbarism, and that nothing could be more natural than for a man still youngish to handle a young girl naked. He thought it natural because he did it every day, and felt and thought, as it seemed to him, no harm as he did it, and consequently he regarded modesty in the girl not merely as a relic of barbarism, but also as an insult to himself.

There was nothing for it but to submit. Though all the doctors had been at the same school, read the same books, and learned the same science, and though some people said this celebrated doctor was actually a bad one, in the princess's household and circle it had somehow been accepted that this celebrated doctor alone had some special knowledge, and that he alone could save Kitty. After a careful examination and sounding of the bewildered patient — who was dazed with shame — the celebrated doctor, having scrupulously washed his hands, stood in the drawing-room talking to the prince. The prince frowned and coughed as he listened. As a man who had seen something of life, no fool and no invalid, he had no faith in medicine, and in his heart was furious at the whole farce, especially since he was perhaps the only one who fully grasped the cause of Kitty's illness. "Conceited blockhead," he thought, listening to the celebrated doctor's chatter about his daughter's symptoms. The doctor, meanwhile, was barely managing to restrain his contempt for this old gentleman, and barely managing to condescend to the level of his intelligence. He could see that talking to the old man was pointless, and that the principal person in the house was the mother. Before her he had decided to cast his pearls. At that moment the princess came into the drawing-room with the family doctor. The prince withdrew, trying not to show how ridiculous he thought the whole performance. The princess was at her wits' end, and did not know what to do. She felt she had sinned against Kitty.
"Well, doctor, decide our fate," the princess said. "Tell me everything."
"Is there hope?" she meant to say, but her lips quivered and she could not utter the question. "Well, doctor?"
"In a moment, princess. I'll talk it over with my colleague, and then I'll have the honor of laying my opinion before you."
"So we had better leave you?"
"As you please."
The princess went out with a sigh.

When the doctors were left alone, the family doctor began timidly explaining his opinion, that there was a beginning of tuberculous trouble, but... and so on. The celebrated doctor listened to him, and in the middle of his sentence looked at his big gold watch.
"Yes," he said. "But..."
The family doctor respectfully stopped in the middle of his observations.

"The beginning of the tuberculous process we are not, as you know, able to define; until there are cavities, there is nothing definite. But we may suspect it. And there are indications: malnutrition, nervous excitability, and so on. The question stands thus: in the presence of indications of a tuberculous process, what is to be done to maintain nutrition?"
"But, you know, there are always moral, spiritual causes at the bottom of these cases," the family doctor allowed himself to interpolate with a subtle smile.

"Yes, that goes without saying," the celebrated physician answered, glancing again at his watch. "Beg pardon, is the Yausky bridge done yet, or will I have to drive round?" he asked. "Ah! It is. Oh well, then I can do it in twenty minutes. So we were saying the problem may be put thus: to maintain nutrition and tone up the nerves. The one is in close connection with the other; one must attack both sides at once."
"And how about a tour abroad?" the family doctor asked.

"I've no liking for foreign tours. And take note: if there is an early stage of tuberculous process, of which we can't be certain, a foreign tour will be of no use. What is wanted is means for improving nutrition, not lowering it." And the celebrated doctor expounded his treatment plan with Soden waters, a remedy obviously prescribed primarily on the grounds that it could do no harm.
The family doctor listened attentively and respectfully.
"But in favor of a foreign trip I would press the change of habits, the removal from surroundings that call up memories. And then the mother wishes it," he added.
"Ah! In that case, to be sure, let them go. Only, those German quacks are mischievous... They'll have to be talked round... Well, let them go, then."
He glanced once more at his watch.
"Oh, time's up already." And he made for the door. The celebrated doctor announced to the princess (a sense of what was due from him made him do it) that he ought to see the patient once more.
"What! Another examination?" the mother cried, with horror.
"Oh, no, only a few details, princess."
"Come this way."

And the mother, accompanied by the doctor, went into the drawing-room to Kitty. Wasted and flushed, with a peculiar glitter in her eyes — left there by the agony of shame she had just been put through — Kitty was standing in the middle of the room. When the doctor came in she flushed crimson, and her eyes filled with tears. All her illness and treatment struck her as so stupid, ludicrous even! Doctoring her seemed to her as absurd as putting together the pieces of a broken vase. Her heart was broken. Why were they trying to cure her with pills and powders? But she could not grieve her mother, especially as her mother considered herself to blame.
"May I trouble you to sit down, princess?" the celebrated doctor said to her.
He sat down with a smile, facing her, took her pulse, and again began putting his tiresome questions to her. She answered him, and all at once stood up, furious.
"Excuse me, doctor, but there's really no point in this. This is the third time you've asked me the same thing."
The celebrated doctor was not offended.
"Nervous irritability," he said to the princess when Kitty had left the room. "However, I had finished..."

And the doctor began scientifically explaining to the princess, as an exceptionally intelligent woman, the condition of the young princess, and concluded by insisting on drinking the waters, which were certainly harmless. To the question whether they should go abroad, the doctor plunged into deep meditation, as if resolving a weighty problem. Finally his decision was pronounced: they were to go abroad, but to put no faith in foreign quacks, and to apply to him in any need.

It was as if some piece of good fortune had come about once the doctor had gone. The mother was much more cheerful when she went back to her daughter, and Kitty pretended to be more cheerful. She had often, almost always, to be pretending now.
"Really, mamma, I'm quite well. But if you want to go abroad, then let's go!" she said, and trying to seem interested in the proposed trip, she began talking about preparations for the journey.
